My friend carefully drove a peg into the ground at the exact place where the beetle had fallen, then took a tape measure from his pocket. He fixed one end to the point on the tree trunk nearest the peg and stretched it out to the peg. From there he continued another fifty feet along the straight line formed by those two points, while Jupiter cut away the brambles with the scythe. He drove a second peg into the spot he reached and marked a rough circle around it, about four feet across. Legrand then took a spade for himself, handed one to Jupiter and another to me, and urged us to start digging as quickly as we could.

In truth, this sort of amusement never appealed much to me. Just then I would have been especially glad to refuse: night was approaching, and our efforts so far had already left me tired. But I could see no way out, and I feared that refusing would upset my poor friend. Had I been able to rely on Jupiter’s help, I would willingly have tried to force the madman to go home. Yet I knew the old black man’s character too well to imagine he would help me struggle with his master under any circumstances. I was certain Legrand had taken up one of the countless Southern superstitions about buried money. Finding the beetle had strengthened this fancy, or perhaps Jupiter’s stubborn claim that it was “a bug of real gold” had done so. Such suggestions could easily mislead someone inclined to madness, particularly when they fitted ideas he already cherished. I then remembered the poor fellow calling the beetle “the guide to his fortune.” All of this left me deeply troubled and confused. At last, though, I decided to make the best of what I could not avoid. I would dig willingly, and so prove sooner, with evidence he could see for himself, that his fanciful beliefs were mistaken.

Once the lanterns were lit, we all began working with an enthusiasm that deserved a more sensible purpose. As their bright light fell across our bodies and tools, I could not help noticing the striking picture we made. I wondered how strange and suspicious our work would look to any intruder who happened to come upon us there.

For two hours we kept steadily digging.

Her position was indeed unusually painful and difficult. As fiercely as she wanted to unravel the mystery surrounding Oliver’s past, she felt bound to respect the confidence the unhappy woman she had just spoken to had placed in her as a young, innocent girl. The woman’s words and manner had moved Rose Maylie deeply. Alongside her love for the boy in her care, and almost equally sincere and passionate, was her tender desire to lead this outcast woman back toward repentance and hope.

They intended to spend only three days in London before leaving for several weeks on a distant stretch of coast. It was already midnight on the first day. What plan could she settle on and carry out within forty-eight hours? And how could she delay their departure without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was staying with them and would remain for the next two days. But Rose knew the good gentleman’s impulsiveness too well. She could too clearly foresee the anger he would direct, in his first burst of indignation, at the person who had helped recapture Oliver. She could not entrust him with the secret when no one with greater experience was there to support her appeal on the girl’s behalf. These same concerns required the greatest care and discretion if she told Mrs. Maylie, whose first reaction would certainly be to discuss the matter with the good doctor. Consulting a lawyer, even had Rose known how to arrange it, was hardly an option for the same reason. Once she thought of asking Harry for help. But that brought back their last separation, and she felt it would be wrong to summon him again when—her eyes filled with tears as she followed the thought—he might already have learned to forget her and found greater happiness away.

Troubled by all these competing thoughts, Rose spent an anxious, sleepless night. She leaned toward one course, then another, only to shrink from every possibility as fresh objections entered her mind. After further debate with herself the following day, desperation finally drove her to decide to consult Harry.

“If returning here is painful for him,” she thought, “how painful it will be for me! But perhaps he won’t come. He might write instead; or he might come himself and take care to avoid seeing me—he did that when he left. I hardly expected him to, but it was better for both of us.” At this Rose let the pen fall and turned away, as if even the paper that would carry her message must not witness her tears.

People who had once been the finest customers anyone could wish for now had not a moment to spare us a thought. They claimed that reading about the revolutions and keeping pace with intellectual progress and the spirit of the times occupied them completely. If a fire needed fanning, a newspaper would do perfectly well. And as the government weakened, leather and iron must, I am sure, have grown correspondingly stronger: before long, not a single pair of bellows in Rotterdam needed a stitch or any attention with a hammer. The situation was unbearable. I soon became desperately poor, and with a wife and children to support, my burdens eventually grew intolerable. I spent hour after hour considering the easiest way to end my life. Meanwhile, debt collectors left me little peace to think. My house was literally under siege from morning until night, until I began to rage, foam, and fret like a caged tiger throwing itself against the bars. Three men in particular harassed me past endurance, constantly watching my door and threatening legal action. Silently I swore to take the bitterest revenge on those three if I ever had the good fortune to get them in my power. I believe nothing but the pleasure of imagining that revenge kept me from immediately carrying out my plan to shoot myself with a blunderbuss. Still, I considered it wiser to conceal my fury and offer them promises and soothing words until some fortunate turn of events gave me my chance for vengeance.

“One day, after slipping away from my creditors and feeling even more despondent than usual, I wandered aimlessly for a long time through the least frequented streets. At last I happened to bump into the corner of a bookseller’s stall. There was a chair nearby for customers; I dropped sullenly into it and, scarcely aware of why I was doing so, opened the first volume within reach. It turned out to be a short pamphlet on Speculative Astronomy, written either by Professor Encke of Berlin or by a Frenchman whose name was rather similar. I already had a slight acquaintance with subjects of this kind. Soon I found myself more and more absorbed in the book, and I actually read the entire thing twice before becoming conscious again of what was happening around me.”
